newsitem.title: UK: Chase sees little U.S. value, likes post-EMU Europe.
newsitem.headline: Chase sees little U.S. value, likes post-EMU Europe.

text.p: Chase Asset Management's chief investment officer said on Friday there was little value left in Wall Street and investors should look to Europe, which will benefit in the runup to a true single market.

Chase, which is the 10th largest money manager in the U.S. with $120 billion worth of assets, has cut allocations to the U.S. and Canadian equity markets to 30.5 percent of a global stocks portfolio compared with 42.0 percent MSCI Index which is used to allocate assets and measure performance.

Mark Richardson told Reuters in an interview that he was surprised only by the size of the decline in the Dow Jones Industrials, which had fallen to 6,330 points by midday trade on Friday from a closing high of 6,606.30 on November 26.

"Classic market theory tells us that this was a market bound for a fall. You can blame anything you like from (Federal Reserve Governor) Alan Greenspan to Iran but this fall was inevitable," Richardson said.
Greenspan warned recently about financial markets' "irrational exuberance", while newspapers reported Saudi Arabia had said Iran was behind the bombing of a U.S. base in June.
"Earnings growth in the U.S. will be weaker through 1997, we expect a fall to eight percent as the ability of U.S. companies to downsize and restructure is limited," Richardson said.
The Dow had risen almost 1,500 points this year at its highest point on benign inflation and economic growth as well as massive money flows ploughed into a roaring bull market.

"In January next year we will see more cash for mutual funds from the baby boomer generation, but most funds have very low levels of liquidity, around 6.25 percent, and will use contributions to add to that rather than invest in stocks," Richardson said.
Chase believes that European Monetary Union will produce the a new league of highly competitive companies.

"With the start of monetary union in 1999, you will have a true single market in which the consumer will have real choice and those companies which have started to plan for that will be huge beneficiaries," Richardson said.
He cited German carmakers Daimler Benz and Volkswagen as two potential benficiaries.

In Japan, which is 15.0 percent of Chase's equity portfolio against 18.2 in the MSCI, the consumer remains unwilling to spend and in the short term only companies with overseas earnings are worth looking at.

"These are the large international blue chips such as Honda, Toyota, Sony and TDK. Honda is finding 112 yen to the dollar to be a competitive exchange rate as they have started exporting from Japan to the U.S. again," Richardson said.
